questions.prompt: Put the basic cookie mechanic in order.
steps: The browser sends a request to the server
The server responds with a `Set-Cookie` header
Every later request to that domain automatically includes the cookie
The server reads the cookie on each request to know who is asking
questions.explanation: Once the server sets the cookie, the browser attaches it to every request to that site automatically, with no JavaScript, until it expires or is cleared.

questions.prompt: How do `UserManager<TUser>` and `SignInManager<TUser>` divide the work?
options: They are alternatives; an app picks one or the other
`UserManager` owns the user record; `SignInManager` owns the act of signing in and is built on top of `UserManager`
`SignInManager` owns the user record; `UserManager` writes the auth cookie
`SignInManager` replaces `UserManager` whenever cookies are used
questions.explanation: `SignInManager` calls into `UserManager` for password and lockout checks, then adds the cookie-writing behaviour on top. They are used together.

questions.prompt: A pure Web API calls `AddIdentity<ApplicationUser, ApplicationRole>()` and then configures JWT bearer auth. Which symptom does the lesson warn about?
options: Passwords are no longer hashed
`UserManager` can't be injected into controllers
Refresh tokens stop rotating
`[Authorize]` redirects to a login page instead of returning 401
questions.explanation: `AddIdentity` silently sets cookies as the default authentication scheme, which competes with JWT bearer. `AddIdentityCore` registers zero authentication schemes, so JWT bearer is the only one in play.

questions.prompt: You switch to `AddIdentityCore<ApplicationUser>()` but still need `RoleManager` and roles. What do you add?
options: `.AddRoles<ApplicationRole>()`
`.AddDefaultTokenProviders()`
`.AddSignInManager()`
Nothing; `AddIdentityCore` includes roles by default
questions.explanation: `AddIdentityCore` registers no role support by default, so you opt back in with the chained `.AddRoles<ApplicationRole>()` call.

questions.prompt: Your app sets a `FallbackPolicy` that requires an authenticated user. Why must the `refresh` endpoint be marked `[AllowAnonymous]`?
options: Because refresh tokens are public and safe to share
Because `[AllowAnonymous]` makes the endpoint faster
Because it exists to issue a new access token after the old one expired; requiring a valid token would make it useless
Because the fallback policy never applies to POST requests
questions.explanation: Endpoints that get a user to an authenticated state (login, register, refresh, reset password and so on) must stay public. Requiring a token to refresh means needing a valid token to get a new token.

questions.prompt: A service reads the current user through `IHttpContextAccessor`, and the same service is reused inside a background job. What does the lesson warn about?
options: `IHttpContextAccessor` can't be injected into services at all
`HttpContext` is `null` outside an HTTP request, so code that doesn't null-check throws a `NullReferenceException`
The background job gets the HttpContext of the last request that ran
`IHttpContextAccessor` is registered as Transient, so each call returns a new HttpContext
questions.explanation: `IHttpContextAccessor.HttpContext` is nullable by design: there is no current request in a background job or hosted service, so always null-check.
